Belial
bē'lĭ-ăl
n. (worthlessness — a Hebrew abstract noun used of the lawless, and by Paul as a name for Satan himself)
From Hebrew Beliya'al, most likely from beli, without, and ya'al, profit or use — hence worthlessness, that which yields nothing. An older suggestion reads it “without going up”, that is, one who never rises. The KJV keeps the Hebrew as a proper name rather than translating it.

Biblical Definition

Belial is not, in the Old Testament, the name of a demon; it is a Hebrew noun meaning worthlessness, and it is nearly always found in the phrases “sons of Belial”, “children of Belial”, or “a man of Belial”. What the phrase describes is a very particular kind of wickedness — not weakness or ignorance but a settled lawlessness that recognises no authority. The instances are ugly and consistent. The mob at Gibeah: “certain sons of Belial beset the house round about, and beat at the door” (Jdg 19:22). The priesthood at Shiloh: “the sons of Eli were sons of Belial; they knew not the LORD” (1Sa 2:12). Abigail on her husband: “this man of Belial, even Nabal: for as his name is, so is he” (1Sa 25:25). The rebel who split the kingdom: “there happened to be there a man of Belial, whose name was Sheba, the son of Bichri” (2Sa 20:1). The false witnesses who killed Naboth were sons of Belial too. By the intertestamental period the word had hardened into a personal name for the evil one, and Paul uses it that way, exactly once, in a passage forbidding covenant fellowship with unbelief: “And what concord hath Christ with Belial? or what part hath he that believeth with an infidel?” (2Co 6:15).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines Belial as a Hebrew word signifying wickedness or worthlessness, and notes that sons of Belial denotes wicked, worthless men, and that Paul uses it of Satan.

expand to see more

BELIAL, n. As a Hebrew word, it signifies unprofitableness, wickedness, worthlessness.

In Scripture, sons or men of Belial are lawless, worthless, wicked men.

It is compounded of beli, without, and yaal, profit or usefulness.

The word is used in the New Testament as a name of Satan, the adversary: what concord hath Christ with Belial?

It denotes not weakness merely, but a settled refusal of all yoke and authority.

Key Scripture

Jdg 19:22 — "Now as they were making their hearts merry, behold, the men of the city, certain sons of Belial, beset the house round about, and beat at the door, and spake to the master of the house, the old man, saying, Bring forth the man that came into thine house, that we may know him."

1Sa 2:12 — "Now the sons of Eli were sons of Belial; they knew not the LORD."

1Sa 25:25 — "Let not my lord, I pray thee, regard this man of Belial, even Nabal: for as his name is, so is he; Nabal is his name, and folly is with him: but I thine handmaid saw not the young men of my lord, whom thou didst send."

2Co 6:15 — "And what concord hath Christ with Belial? or what part hath he that believeth with an infidel?"

Modern Corruption

Wickedness is redefined as damage or dysfunction, categories that call for treatment; Belial names it as worthlessness before God — a moral and not a therapeutic verdict.

expand to see more

The word Belial cuts directly across the modern moral vocabulary, which is why it sounds so strange now. Contemporary language for evil is drawn from medicine and injury: behaviour is unhealthy, damaging, or the product of unmet need, and the remedy is treatment and understanding. Scripture's category here is different in kind. Beliya'al is a verdict of worthlessness — a man who yields no profit, who has thrown off the yoke, who “knew not the LORD”. The men of Gibeah were not unwell; the sons of Eli were not under-resourced. The Bible does have deep compassion for the afflicted, and it distinguishes carefully between the sinned-against and the sinner. But it will not let the distinction dissolve the category of the wicked, because a man who cannot be called wicked cannot be called to repent, and a doctrine of sin is the only ground on which forgiveness can be offered.

The other thing to hold is the phrase Paul quarries out of it. 2Co 6:15 sits in the passage that begins “Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers”, and the argument is a series of questions with only one answer: righteousness with unrighteousness, light with darkness, Christ with Belial, the temple of God with idols. Paul is not forbidding contact with unbelievers — he had already told the same church that this would require going out of the world. He is forbidding the yoke: the binding partnership, the shared enterprise, the marriage, in which a believer's course is tied to an unbeliever's. The old Hebrew word for a man with no yoke turns up in the New Testament to warn believers about the yokes they choose.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Beliya'al (H1100), worthlessness, from beli (H1097), without, and ya'al (H3276), to profit; Greek Belial (G955).

expand to see more

Hebrew Beliya'al (H1100) — Belial; worthlessness, destruction, wickedness.

Hebrew beli (H1097) — without, failure, nothing; the negative particle in the compound.

Hebrew ya'al (H3276) — to profit, to be of use; the second element, giving “good for nothing”.

Hebrew ben-Beliya'al — “son of Belial”; a Hebrew idiom of character, as “son of peace” or “sons of thunder”.

Greek Belial (G955) — Belial; used once, of Satan, in 2Co 6:15.

Usage

"“Certain sons of Belial beset the house” — the mob at Gibeah."

"“The sons of Eli were sons of Belial; they knew not the LORD” — the verdict on a priesthood."

"“What concord hath Christ with Belial?” — a question with only one answer."
